```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.6)
library(mssrscopR)
show <- function(m, main) {
  graphics::image(t(m[nrow(m):1, ]), col = grDevices::gray.colors(128, 0, 1),
                  axes = FALSE, main = main, cex.main = 0.9, asp = nrow(m) / ncol(m))
}
```

All images here are synthetic and generated in this document, so the true
scene is known.

## The operator

Mean-Shift Super-Resolution (MSSR; Torres-García et al. 2022,
doi:10.1038/s41467-022-34693-9) subtracts a local, range-weighted mean-shift
estimate from each pixel and refines the result over `order` steps. `fwhm` is
the point-spread-function width in **input pixels** and has no default.

```{r points}
g <- expand.grid(r = 1:31, c = 1:41)
spot <- function(r0, c0, a = 1) a * exp(-((g$r - r0)^2 + (g$c - c0)^2) / (2 * (3 / 2.3548)^2))
pair <- function(sep) matrix(spot(16, 18) + spot(16, 18 + sep) + 0.05, 31, 41)
x <- pair(3)                       # two sources 3 px apart, FWHM 3 px
res <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
res
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
show(x, "input"); show(as.matrix(res), "mssr(amp = 2)")
par(op)
```

The amplified grid only adds samples. `mssr_coords()` places them in
input-pixel units, and the field of view stays `[0.5, n + 0.5]`:

```{r coords}
range(mssr_coords(res)$col)
res$transform$spacing
```

How far does the separation go? Compare the value at the midpoint between the
two sources with the value at a source center, in the input and in the MSSR
map (values below 1 mean a dip between the sources):

```{r separation}
mid_ratio <- function(sep) {
  x <- pair(sep)
  r <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
  v <- as.matrix(r)
  co <- mssr_coords(r)
  row <- which.min(abs(co$row - 16))
  at_input <- function(cc) stats::approx(1:41, x[16, ], cc)$y
  at_mssr <- function(cc) stats::approx(co$col, v[row, ], cc)$y
  c(input = at_input(18 + sep / 2) / at_input(18), mssr = at_mssr(18 + sep / 2) / at_mssr(18))
}
round(rbind(`2.4 px` = mid_ratio(2.4), `2.6 px` = mid_ratio(2.6), `3 px` = mid_ratio(3)), 3)
```

At 3 px the input shows only a shallow dip, which MSSR deepens strongly. At
2.6 px the input pixels have a single maximum, between the sources, yet MSSR
returns two peaks with a clear dip (ratio below 1): it can separate sources that
the pixels show merged. Its peaks move toward each other, so a ratio taken at the
source centers can stay above 1 although two peaks exist. The peak positions
along row 16 show this directly (true sources at 18 and 18 + separation):

```{r peaks}
peaks <- function(sep, amp = 2) {
  r <- mssr(pair(sep), fwhm = 3, amp = amp)
  co <- mssr_coords(r)
  v <- as.matrix(r)[which.min(abs(co$row - 16)), ]
  i <- which(diff(sign(diff(v))) == -2) + 1
  co$col[i[v[i] > 0.05 * max(v)]]
}
list(`2.4 px` = peaks(2.4), `2.4 px, amp 4` = peaks(2.4, amp = 4), `2.6 px` = peaks(2.6))
```

At 2.4 px MSSR returns a single, sharper peak at `amp = 2`; at `amp = 4` it shows
two peaks with a barely visible dip, 1 px apart for sources 2.4 px apart. The
spacing of MSSR peaks therefore underestimates the true separation near this
limit.

## Known failure modes

MSSR is nonlinear. A dim structure next to a bright one is strongly
suppressed, and broad filled objects can be hollowed or fragmented:

```{r failures}
y <- matrix(spot(16, 14) + spot(16, 21.5, 0.1) + 0.02, 31, 41)   # 10:1 brightness
disk <- outer(1:31, 1:41, function(r, c) as.numeric((r - 16)^2 + (c - 21)^2 <= 81))
disk <- disk + 0.02
ry <- as.matrix(mssr(y, fwhm = 3))
rd <- as.matrix(mssr(disk, fwhm = 3))
c(input_ratio = y[16, 22] / y[16, 14], mssr_ratio = ry[16, 22] / ry[16, 14],
  disk_center = rd[16, 21])
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
show(ry, "dim beside bright"); show(disk, "filled disk"); show(rd, "mssr(disk)")
par(op)
```

Extended objects are emphasized at their edges: the filled disk becomes a ring
with a zero center, so segment filled objects such as nuclei on the original
data. A rod three FWHM long becomes two peaks near its ends, with a lower
interior:

```{r rod}
rod <- matrix(Reduce(`+`, lapply(seq(16.5, 25.5, length.out = 41),
                                 function(cc) spot(16, cc, 1 / 41))) + 0.002, 31, 41)
rr <- mssr(rod, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
co <- mssr_coords(rr)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(co$col, as.matrix(rr)[which.min(abs(co$row - 16)), ], type = "l",
     xlab = "column (input px)", ylab = "mssr along row 16")
lines(1:41, rod[16, ] / max(rod[16, ]) * max(rr$values), lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("mssr", "input (scaled)"), lty = 1:2, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

With noise, the mean shift also responds to noise maxima: single sources and
short rods can break into several peaks, one source can look like a pair, and
dim sources are lost first. An `fwhm` smaller than the true PSF makes false
pairs more likely, and higher `order` values add further, mostly weak, maxima. Compare results with the
input, and test settings on a synthetic noisy scene of known content that
resembles your data.

These failure modes are why the outputs are **not quantitative**;
`res$diagnostics$quantitative` is always `FALSE`.

## Several channels or bands

`mssr()` takes one 2D frame, so multichannel and spectral data are processed one
channel at a time, and each channel gets its own structure map. Here channel `b`
holds the same two sources as channel `a`, but its second source is half as
bright; `0.5 * a` is a scaled copy of `a`:

```{r channels}
a <- matrix(spot(16, 14) + spot(16, 26) + 0.05, 31, 41)
b <- matrix(spot(16, 14) + spot(16, 26, 0.5) + 0.05, 31, 41)
ra <- as.matrix(mssr(a, fwhm = 3))
rb <- as.matrix(mssr(b, fwhm = 3))
rc <- as.matrix(mssr(0.5 * a, fwhm = 3))
round(c(input = b[16, 26] / a[16, 26], mssr = rb[16, 26] / ra[16, 26],
        scaled_copy = rc[16, 26] / ra[16, 26]), 3)
```

The ratio of `b` to `a` at the second source falls to about half its input
value, while the scaled copy keeps its ratio. A different background or another
object elsewhere in one channel also changes the ratios. Ratios between
channels, indices and spectra therefore belong to the original data, for example
measured under a mask as below.

## Masks with measurements on the original data

A structure map can select pixels, but measurements belong to the original
image. `mssr_mask()` keeps an exact number of pixels of a region.
`tie_fraction` reports the share of the selected pixels that random
tie-breaking decided. That share can be large, because the mean shift is
clipped at zero and many pixels tie there.

```{r mask}
m <- mssr_mask(mssr(x, fwhm = 3), fraction = 0.2)
c(coverage = attr(m, "coverage"), tie_fraction = attr(m, "tie_fraction"))
c(mean_all = mean(x), mean_masked = mean(x[m]))
```

Selecting pixels this way changes the measured population. It is not known to
improve any downstream analysis, so evaluate it for your own task.

## Degenerate input and unsupported requests

Flat frames return zeros flagged as degenerate. Requests the package cannot
honor fail with classed errors:

```{r errors}
mssr(matrix(1, 5, 5), fwhm = 3)$diagnostics[c("degenerate", "degenerate_reason")]
try(mssr(array(0, c(4, 4, 3)), fwhm = 3))     # no axis is guessed
try(mssr(matrix(c(1, NA, 3, 4), 2), fwhm = 3)) # non-finite input
```

## Interactive exploration

`mssr_app()` opens the same computations in a Shiny app (it needs the shiny,
bslib, jsonlite, callr and digest packages). It shows the input and the structure map on the
same input-pixel axes, line profiles, masks measured on the input and the
self-test, and offers the results for download. The examples above are
available there, and frames can be uploaded as text tables, PNG or TIFF.

Computation runs in one background job per app session. Cancel stops the owned
job, and incomplete results cannot be exported. A previous completed input,
settings and mask can be explicitly restored. The run record distinguishes
restored results and settings captured at computation from current controls.
A session closing or a five-minute limit stops its unfinished job. Development
source launches need pkgload; installed-package launches use the exact installed
namespace and verify their loaded definitions.

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
mssr_app()
```

## Checking an installation

`mssr_selftest()` recomputes the bundled synthetic fixtures. They were produced
by the package's engine definition, so this is a regression check of the
installation, not an independent validation:

```{r selftest}
st <- mssr_selftest()
st[, c("fixture_id", "max_abs_error", "passed")]
```

## Reproducible expert workflow

Choose FWHM from the acquisition PSF in input-pixel units. Record its source and
uncertainty; an image's dimensions do not establish physical calibration. A
measured PSF is preferable to a theoretical one, which describes an ideal
system; the recorded PSF can be wider. Under noise a too-small FWHM adds false
peaks and a larger one weakens the separation of close sources, so choose the
larger plausible value when unsure. Only the kernel half-size in
`parameters$half_size` enters the computation, so compare settings that change
it. Fix preprocessing, channel selection, frame boundaries and parameter-selection rules
before evaluating outcomes. Cropping changes the neighborhood context and global
normalizers, so a cropped reconstruction need not equal a crop of the full-frame
result. Background subtraction is a distinct preprocessing decision.

Start with a low order and compare plausible acquisition-informed settings.
Orders above 3 are accepted for compatibility but produce a qualification warning:
the expanded independent reference suite found sensitive high-order failures.
The bounded passing domain is evidence about the tested scenes, not a guarantee
for an arbitrary noisy acquisition. Review broad-object hollowing/splitting,
missing dim structures and blank/noise-only fields alongside favorable examples.

```{r expert-inspection}
frame <- outer(1:13, 1:17, function(r, c) 0.05 + exp(-((r-7)^2+(c-9)^2)/8))
result <- mssr(frame, fwhm = 3, order = 1)
summary(result)
mssr_estimate_resources(dim(frame), fwhm = 3)
```

`mssr_validate_result()` checks a result's internal contract. `mssr_write_result()`
and `mssr_read_result()` use explicit paths, integrity hashes and exact binary
values; optional `digest` and `jsonlite` are needed for these operations. They do
not establish acquisition provenance. Never use reconstructed intensities as
calibrated measurements. Original-data measurements under a mask still reflect
selection bias: report retained coverage, compare with sensible controls and
inspect how small score changes alter the selected population.

`mssr_batch()` processes a named list of independent whole frames with one worker.
It records failures and cancellations, checks completed results before reuse and
retains separate attempts. It checks cancellation between frames. Its memory
budget is a conservative estimate; use a separate process-level limit when a
hard memory cap is required. It does not implement tiling or infer time, depth,
wavelength, specimen identity or physical units from an array.

## Save and replay an analysis

`mssr_settings()` validates the result and returns only callable computation
settings, including the grid. Passing `result$parameters` directly is not a
replay recipe: it includes a derived kernel half-size and omits the grid.
Settings are resolved values, so mesh compensation is recorded as off when
amplification is 1. Resource budgets are not retained settings; choose them
explicitly when recomputing.

The example below retains the original synthetic frame and mask context in
memory, then reads the exact result from a file. For a durable analysis, keep
the original frame in trusted storage and retain its identity, preprocessing,
channel/frame selection, acquisition information and mask context alongside it.
The `.mssr` file does not contain those inputs. Here no acquisition calibration
is available, and FWHM is a chosen synthetic setting.

```{r replay-analysis}
original <- frame
context <- list(
  preprocessing = "none; authored synthetic frame",
  region = outer(seq_len(nrow(original)), seq_len(ncol(original)),
                 function(r, c) r <= 10 & c >= 4),
  fraction = 0.2,
  seed = 23L
)
result <- mssr(original, fwhm = 3, amp = 2, order = 1,
               max_output_pixels = 5e7, max_memory_bytes = 1024^3)
mask <- mssr_mask(result, fraction = context$fraction,
                  region = context$region, seed = context$seed)
measurement <- mean(original[mask])

if (requireNamespace("digest", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".mssr")
  mssr_write_result(result, path)
  restored <- mssr_read_result(path)
  stopifnot(identical(restored$engine$package_version,
                      as.character(packageVersion("mssrscopR"))))
  replay <- do.call(mssr, c(
    list(x = original, max_output_pixels = 5e7, max_memory_bytes = 1024^3),
    mssr_settings(restored)
  ))
  replay_mask <- mssr_mask(replay, fraction = context$fraction,
                           region = context$region, seed = context$seed)
  stopifnot(identical(replay$values, restored$values),
            identical(replay$transform, restored$transform),
            identical(replay_mask, mask),
            identical(mean(original[replay_mask]), measurement))
  unlink(path)
}
```

Preserve the package artifact and runtime environment with a durable analysis,
for example by retaining `sessionInfo()` output. The helper refuses results from
a different numerical engine and does not migrate historical results. A legacy
result schema with the current engine can still supply validated settings.
Matching engine and settings is not a promise of identical arithmetic across
package versions or environments: verify values and the original-data
measurement after replay. The measurement remains subject to mask selection;
successful reproduction does not validate the scientific choice of mask.
